Benny Waters lays claim to be the oldest working jazzman in the country, probably in the world. Born in Maryland in 1902, Benny showed an early musical aptitude, giving piano recitals by age seven, and soon after learning the reed instruments from his older brother. He played in dance bands while still in high school and attended the Boston Conservatory of Music where he studied piano and theory while teaching clarinet. After leaving Boston, Benny found work with Charlie Johnson’s Paradise Orchestra, leading to gigs at Small’s Paradise in Harlem where he associated with great artists like Louis Armstrong. Starting in 1933, Benny played for ten years in the bands of Fletcher Henderson, Jimmie Lunceford and Hot Lips Page. A visit to Europe with Jimmy Archey led to a stay of almost 40 years and he became a senior member of Europe’s American jazz community. Benny worked with various groups in Paris until he struck out on his own at the age of 67 and toured Europe with the occasional visit to the U.S. These visits became more frequent and eventually led to Benny’s settling back in the homeland in 1992. His is a frequent performer on numerous jazz radio programs and a member of the newly-formed Statesmen of Jazz.
Benny was interviewed in Los Angeles, on September 1, 1995 by Michael Woods.
Hamilton College Jazz Archive are filming interviews with America’s greatest jazz musicians. We have here the elderstatesman of jazz, Benny Waters. Pleased to have you, Benny.
Well thank you. I’m happy to be here.
